label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 4 — Psalms 73–89
summary_plain: Psalms 73 through 89 grapple with YHWH's faithfulness in the face of national catastrophe. Psalm 73 asks: why do the wicked prosper? But Asaf enters the sanctuary and understands their end. Psalm 78 retells the whole covenant history from Mitzrayim to Dawid. Psalm 83 is the cry of alarm: the nations conspire together — they say, come, let us wipe them out as a nation, let the name of Yisra'EL be remembered no more. Psalm 89 recites YHWH's covenant with Dawid: I will establish your throne forever. Then it cries out: but you have renounced the covenant of your servant — how long, O YHWH?
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalms 73-89 from DSS witnesses and the Orit Ge'ez. Psalm 83 is the single most precise verse in all scripture describing the systematic erasure of Israelite identity — a coalition of nations making a covenant specifically to ensure the name of Yisra'EL is remembered no more. The psalm names the confederates: Edom, the Yishma'elim, Mo'av, the Hagrim, Geval, Ammon, Amaleq, Pelesheth, Tzor, and Ashur. Psalm 89 is the Dawid covenant psalm — YHWH swears an oath that Dawid's throne is eternal, then the psalmist laments that the covenant appears broken. The tension between promise and present reality is the theological engine of the exile psalms. The DSS community at Qumran lived in this tension — they preserved both the promise and the lament without resolving the contradiction through institutional theology.

key_terms.definition: The only psalm attributed to Moshe; opens Book IV. Reflects on YHWH's eternity versus human transience: 'A thousand years in your sight are like a watch in the night.'
'For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night.' YHWH's time is not human time; divine patience is not delay.

key_terms.term: Psalm 91 Shelter of the Most High
key_terms.definition: The great psalm of divine protection: 'He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.' Promises angelic protection, rescue from pestilence and snare, and covenant security.

'For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.' Ancient source; NT writers borrowed this verse — it appears in the wilderness temptation narrative of their invented figure. The original context is covenant protection for those who trust in YHWH.
An enthronement psalm: 'Sing to YHWH a new song; sing to YHWH, all the earth.' Declares YHWH's glory among the nations and YHWH's coming to judge the earth in righteousness.

key_terms.term: Psalm 103 Bless YHWH O My Soul
key_terms.definition: David's psalm of YHWH's covenant love: forgiveness, healing, redemption, coronation with love and mercy, satisfaction with good things. 'Bless YHWH, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name.'

'As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.' YHWH's forgiveness is complete, directional, unbounded — east and west never converge, so the transgressions are removed to infinite distance.

The 'Egyptian Hallel' — six psalms (113-118) sung at Pesakh, Shavuot, Sukkot, and Khanukkah. The name 'Egyptian Hallel' refers to Ps.114's reference to the Exodus from Mitzrayim. Used liturgically at the Passover seder.

Another name for the Hallel cycle (Ps.113-118) used at the three pilgrim festivals and Khanukkah; called 'Egyptian' because Psalm 114 begins 'When Yisra'el went out of Mitzrayim.' The seder's Hallel is taken from these psalms.

Psalm 90 carries the unique superscription 'A Prayer of Moshe, the man of YHWH' — the only psalm attributed to Moshe in the canonical Psalter. It opens Book IV with a reflection on YHWH's eternity as the answer to Ps.89's lament over human failure.

faq.question: Why is Psalm 90 attributed to Moshe and what does it contribute to Book IV?
faq.answer: Psalm 90 is the Psalter's only psalm attributed to Moshe — a figure predating the monarchy entirely. Book IV (Ps.90-106) opens by going back past David's dynasty to YHWH's eternal existence. It answers Book III's closing lament (Ps.89's crisis over the Davidic covenant) by lifting the view: YHWH was Israel's dwelling place before kingdoms, and will be after. Human dynasties fail; YHWH's eternity is the constant.

faq.question: What does Psalm 90:4 teach about YHWH's experience of time?
faq.answer: Psalm 90:4 states that a thousand years are to YHWH like yesterday once it has passed — a completed unit that is gone — or like a watch in the night, a few brief hours. YHWH does not experience time as humans do: what feels like infinite delay to a human is a brief moment to YHWH. This reframes the community's impatience and complaint — YHWH's slowness is not indifference but a different relationship with time altogether.

faq.question: What is Psalm 91 about and who is the 'shelter of the Most High'?
faq.answer: Psalm 91 is the great protective psalm of the Psalter, promising comprehensive divine protection to the one who makes YHWH their refuge and dwelling. The 'shelter of the Most High' is YHWH's protective presence — not necessarily a physical place but the covenantal relationship of trust that makes YHWH's care operative. The promises are covenant promises, not unconditional magic.

faq.question: How did NT writers borrow from Psalm 91:11 and what is the original meaning?
faq.answer: NT writers placed Psalm 91:11 on the lips of their adversary figure during a 'temptation' scene — quoting it to suggest the invented figure could throw himself from the Temple and angels would catch him. The original context in Psalm 91 is about covenant protection for the person who trusts in YHWH in daily life — protection from snares, pestilence, and attack. Using it as a proof-text for a stunt inverts its meaning.

faq.question: What does Psalm 96 declare about YHWH's relationship to all nations?
faq.answer: Psalm 96 is a universal enthronement psalm — YHWH's glory is to be declared among all nations; all gods of the peoples are powerless (elilim — worthless things); YHWH made the heavens. YHWH is coming to judge the earth in righteousness and faithfulness. The psalm commands universal worship — not Yisra'el alone but all families of the nations are to attribute glory and strength to YHWH.

faq.question: What are the key themes of Psalm 103?
faq.answer: Psalm 103 catalogues YHWH's covenant benefits: forgiveness of all iniquity, healing of disease, redemption from the pit, coronation with love and mercy, satisfaction with good things, renewal of youth like an eagle. The psalm then grounds these personal benefits in YHWH's covenant character: compassionate as a parent, knowing our dust-nature, removing transgressions as far as east from west. It closes with a cosmic call to all angels and all creation to bless YHWH.

faq.question: What does the 'east from west' comparison in Psalm 103:12 mean?
faq.answer: East and west are directions that never converge — they recede from each other infinitely. YHWH's removal of transgressions is compared to this: once removed, they are placed at an unbounded distance. The comparison makes forgiveness total and directional — the transgressions are not merely overlooked or suspended, they are actively moved to the furthest possible distance from the person.

faq.question: What is the Egyptian Hallel and when was it used?
faq.answer: The Egyptian Hallel is Psalms 113-118, used liturgically at the three great pilgrimage festivals (Pesakh, Shavuot, Sukkot) and Khanukkah. The name 'Egyptian' comes from Psalm 114's opening reference to Yisra'el's departure from Mitzrayim. At Pesakh, Psalms 113-114 were sung before the meal and 115-118 after. These are the psalms that were part of the last Passover seder observance described in the accounts — 'when they had sung the hymn, they went out.'

faq.question: How do Psalms 105 and 106 function as a pair at the end of Book IV?
faq.answer: Psalm 105 retells the covenant history from YHWH's side — YHWH's faithfulness to the promise made to Avraham, the preservation of Yosef, the plagues of Mitzrayim, the wilderness provision. Psalm 106 retells the same history from the people's side — rebellion, idolatry, ingratitude. Together they form a diptych: YHWH's faithfulness against human unfaithfulness throughout history. Book IV closes with this honest reckoning, then Book V begins with a great 'give thanks to YHWH' (Ps.107).

faq.question: Why does Psalm 90 begin Book IV rather than a Davidic psalm?
faq.answer: Book III ended with Psalm 89's lament over the apparent abandonment of the Davidic covenant — the crown in the dust, enemies mocking. Book IV answers this crisis not with more Davidic psalms but by going back to Moshe and YHWH's pre-monarchic existence. The editorial placement says: when dynasties fail, the community's true refuge is YHWH's eternal nature, not any human covenant arrangement. YHWH was dwelling place before David and remains so after.
